pr_body: This is a follow up to https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/pull/25951 The idea here is to allow `public` posts by `discoverable` users to show up in search results. This is done by adding a new Public Status Index to Elastic Search. A status is added to the `PublicStatusesIndex` if the status's visibility is `public` and if the account is `discoverable`. Note: This will only work on instances with Elastic Search enabled. ## Outstanding questions 1. I'm not really sure how to test the changes to the Mastodon CLI. How do I do that? Can someone point me in the right direction there? 2. I'm also not sure how to know if the vacuum changes are working. 3. I wanted to add a few more tests for the `AccountStatusesSearch` concern, but I think I might need to add a new gem to do that (`chewy_spec`). I'm not sure what the process is for adding new gems. Is that something I can just do, or perhaps if there is a conversation that should happen first. ## Examples Two `public` posts were made. One from a `discoverable` account and one from a `non-discoverable` account. You can see both of these posts in the `StatusesIndex` However, you can only see one of these posts, the one by the `discoverable` account, in the `PublicStatusesIndex` Any random user can then search for the string `hello` and only the public post will be returned from that search query ## Account Deletion An account creates a public post When/if that account is deleted, so are its posts. ## Discoverable --> Non-discoverable If a `discoverable` account posts something And then switches the `discoverability` of their account, the posts are removed from the `public` index ## Non-discoverable --> Discoverable But if they then post again and then switch back, all the posts are returned to the index ___ Fixes MAS-88
pr_comments:
I think this is a good *option* to have, e.g. for artists who want to be discovered by their posts beyond just the hashtags they pick (though hashtags remain important for instances that don't have Elasticsearch enabled).

**However**, the `discoverable` flag/`Suggest account to others` option controls a lot of features.  Especially of note, this is a significant change to how the `discoverable` option previously worked, which may negatively surprise folks.

1.  Could we make a new, separate setting for opting in to full-text search, perhaps as a sub-setting to discoverability?

2.  Alternatively, perhaps this should be tied to the setting for `Opt-out of search engine indexing`..?  Given this is indexing your public statuses in a search engine, only it is Mastodon that acts as the search engine, not a third party.

(In my case, I may be comfortable having folks discover my account based on my profile, but I am less comfortable about full-text search across all my public posts.  I realize that third-parties can and do disregard that, but I feel Mastodon should set the gold standard for user privacy/control.)

It is my decision to unite all discovery features in one setting, because all of this stuff is an expected part of a social network and splitting it up into different settings that everyone has to opt-into one by one just to get the same behaviour they get by default on other social media seems like a bad user experience. Also, `discoverable` is already a federated attribute.

I've added the following search modifiers:

- `has:image`
- `has:video`
- `has:audio`
- `has:media`
- `has:poll`
- `has:link`
- `has:embed`
- `is:sensitive`
- `is:reply`
- `language:en`
- `before:2023-08-08`
- `after:2023-08-08`
- `during:2023-08-08`

I've change the default query operator from `OR` to `AND` (this renders the `+` prefix obsolete, though) and the sorting of results to chronological. That way the results are easier to navigate.

I understand the appeal to sticking everything behind `discoverable`. However, I think the reality is that many people will turn off discoverability due to this feature. I don’t think it’s a win to users to have less of the Mastodon network be discoverable through other means, just because some people don’t want randos showing up in their replies. Letting people have partial discoverability will increase the total number of discoverable accounts on the platform.

I am genuinely bamboozled by how the main author of this software, the embracing of which was largely on the back of people trying to take back control of their data and privacy, has decided to completely about-face and justify privacy concessions and the continual removal/deprecation of user control/configurability, and introduction of more and more features without any ability to cleanly disable them for admins.

The sheer cheek of justifying every change as “it matches the expectations of other social media”, when that social media is exactly what is crumbling, enshittified, squeezing the last valuable bits of user data out to pay off investors while getting continually worse to use.

It’s like pointing to Grenfell Tower, and saying “we’re building our building with the same cheap flammable cladding, because it’s what renters expect.”
The users have been been trained on capitalist, value-extracting patterns, with no other choices. Of course they expect it. Some of them are confused when that isn't the case. What’s even the point of this project if you’re just trying to be the downstream reimplementation of Twitter.

Soon enough, mastodon.social will be hard-coded as the serving domain because “that matches the expectations of other social media platforms”.

In case it’s not clear:
implement this feature if you like. But if there isn’t a direct instance-level admin off-switch, *and* per-user opt-*in*, it is a deeply dishonest rug-pull by utterly deviating from the current expectations of the privacy of their posts, that disproportionately affects marginalised groups who are most often targeted for dogpiling & harassment.

A consent-based option allowing people who want their posts to be added to search engines is a good thing -- I think most people will choose to opt in for most of their posts.  However I have some concerns with the specific iinitial mplementation here

- it's not clear to me whether it's opt-in or opt-out for new accounts.  Do they start with discoverable = true?

- The text on the preference page says "Suggest account to others (recommended)." People who have made choices on this option were not told that it would determine whether or not their public posts get added to search engines.  So existing settings are not informed consent.

Adding a separate "search-indexable" property, defaulting to false, gets around both of these  problem -- as well as addressing the issue @marrus-sh mentioned above and providing the ability to fix the problem about posts being added to google even if you've selected the "don't add posts to search engines" https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/issues/22047

Alternatively, you could unify the discoverable to be an enum with choices "none", "suggest accounts",  and "suggest accounts and include in search engines".  As part of the upgrade, existing accounts would have to be reset to "suggest accounts".  The default for new accounts should be either "none" or "suggest accounts", matching today's behavior; it could also make sense to provide an option for admins to change the default for their instance, although it would have to be disclosed to people signing up.
Discoverable is false by default (i.e. opt-in). The hint on the option says: "Allow your account to be discovered by strangers through recommendations, trends and other features".

Eugen, you said, "It is my decision to unite all discovery features in one setting, because all of this stuff is an expected part of a social network..." And I want you to take a moment and realize that a lot of us joined the Fediverse *because* it was different.

I set Discoverable to true on my profile because I wanted people to find me and take a look. Not to search every public toot I make for certain words. Some people who are on instances that basically already have this patched in search their own names or instance domains and butt into conversations that weren't directed to them. It's already being used for harassment.

Between the Discovery "catch all" flag, the way the Local feed is hidden in the apps, and how unlisted posts isn't an option in the apps, you're threatening to kill the "local community" feel Mastodon has provided until now. I'm concerned - as are many others, I feel - that under this new direction Mastodon is killing the individual servers & communities and moving to simply distributing *costs* of running *your* social network.

Sure, the search system in its current form works for some, but it's a UX nightmare for others. Safety and privacy of users is important, definitely, but having a good user experience and safety aren't mutually exclusive of each other. issue_context.title: Replies to posts can be indexed by search engines even if I've opted out of search engine indexing
issue_context.body:
### Steps to reproduce the problem

1. Check the "opt-out of search engine indexing" option (Preferences/Other)
2. Make a public or unlisted reply to a public post by somebody who doesn't have that option checked
3. Wait for search engines to pick up that public post 
4. Use Google (or another search engine) to search for the content in your reply.  [Here's an example of a successful search using the text of an unlisted reply](https://www.google.com/search?q=%22one+gets+recognition+for+getting+a+lot+of+papers+and+also+for+attracting+a+lot+of+funds%22&client=ubuntu&hs=Dwm&channel=fs&sxsrf=ALiCzsb1tJVej1vsfJL-gGBhbVlueyP_iQ%3A1670136729744&ei=mUOMY-uHLZPA7gKBoI7gBQ&ved=0ahUKEwiruIKUsN_7AhUToFsKHQGQA1wQ4dUDCA8&uact=5&oq=%22one+gets+recognition+for+getting+a+lot+of+papers+and+also+for+attracting+a+lot+of+funds%22) -- thanks @dariusk !
...

### Expected behaviour

Google shouldn't return a link to a page with my post on it -- because I've opted-out of search engine indexing" should opt me out of search engine indexing

### Actual behaviour

Google returns the public post I replied to, with my reply on the page

### Detailed description

Checking the "opt-out of search engine indexing" should opt my posts out of indexing by search engines.  It doesn't. 

The description says that this option "Affects your public profile and post pages", and so people who are familiar enough with how federation and search engine's "noindex" directive works could figure out that this doesn't really opt you out. For most people, however, clicking the option just gives a false sense of security.

Either the behavior should be fixed to truly opt posts out of search engine results, or the option should be reworded to give a more accurate description -- "Include my profile in search engine results", for example.

#13207 is a related but more general bug.


### Specifications

Mastodon 4.0.2
comments: This is unfortunately a difficult problem to solve, as there's no way to tell search engines to ignore *part* of a webpage.

Thanks, @ineffyble. Since the UI knows the "noindex" status of the main toot and also that of each reply, would it be too crazy for UI to simply exclude from rendering "noindex" reply toots on an indexable toot page unless the user is authenticated?

replies_to_render = replies_to_render.filter( (d) -> toot.author.noindex || user.authenticated || !d.author.noindex )

It could make threads look very weird to remote/unauthenticated users, if random posts aren't rendered but replies to them are.

But another big problem is that the indexing preference is not federated, so even if you did this, it would only help where both the original post and the reply post are on the same instance.
Understood.  Thank you for the explanation.

I didn't realize the "noindex" wasn't federated, that's certainly an issue.  Thanks for the info.

If it really can't be fixed then I recommend taking the option away (or maybe renaming it). The situation right now is the worst of all worlds: people *think* they're protected, but they aren't.

I would strongly suggest to completely remove this option as it gives a false sense of privacy.

Recent discussions in the Fediverse around search engines show impressively how this feature is misunderstood by users. This option is only setting the "noindex" meta tag on the profile page, but it does NOT prevent the profile from being indexed by other Mastodon instances.

Another problem is that this option has (almost) no impact on indexing by Google, although Google fully respects this option. Toots and profile information are not just displayed on the users profile page. If a post contains a tag, the post will also appear on the tag page. If a user has at least one follower on a remote instance, the toots will be federated there and be displayed on the federated timeline of the remote instance, from which Google will pick it up. Toots can also be boosted, or replied to, or...
Toots are simply displayed on too many pages to be able to hold up with the promise that they do not end up in Google.

I described this specific problem together with other privacy concerns here:
https://medium.com/@s.kopf/mastodon-is-a-zero-privacy-network-here-is-what-you-need-to-know-86aeed685e41
With #26344 federating a new opt-in setting for whether somebody wants their posts searchable, this is now fixable (using the new flag instead).

> With #26344 federating a new opt-in setting for whether somebody wants their posts searchable, this is now fixable (using the new flag instead).

I haven't fully reviewed that PR yet, so I don't know what federates yet, but I have something to add here: having the information is only one part of the solution, the issue is that we can't tell search engines that some part of the page is not to be indexed. I have not found a way yet to exclude replies/parent posts from search results without also making them completely unavailable to logged-out users.

Might we best let go of the idea that we present threads at all to unauthenticated users (which are in general a mix of *discoverable* and *not discoverable* posts), and simply present the one individual post for which the post URL refers, assuming that that one post is discoverable?   

That way the search result would give the searcher exactly what they asked for, and if they wanted to see more context, they could log in. 

The analogy for me is that of the embedded tweet - I see just the one (discoverable) tweet, not the entire thread.  If I click on it and log in (or am already logged in), I see the whole thread.

I'd be OK with that.  I realize its a "strong" UI choice rather than a minimal change from the current implementation.  But imagine that it were behind a server feature flag, and admins had a conversation with their community like "We have the choice to present search engines and unauthenticated users with just those posts that their authors have elected to be discoverable, or we can  present search engines and unauthenticated users with those posts in their thread context, which means that users who have opted out of discoverability will see their posts indexed because they engaged in a thread with a discoverable post."   (I'm assuming the "enforcement" of discoverability is totally up to client implementations, which is itself weak soup, but I may be off base here).  

This might strike an acceptable balance between discoverability and safety.

On the other hand, an indexed toot with its thread that looks like:

```
https://server/user/2

--------------------------
Toot 1 text
--------------------------
|
--------------------------
TOOT 2 TEXT 
--------------------------
|
--------------------------
_Log_in_ to read this toot
--------------------------
|
--------------------------
Toot 4 text
--------------------------
```

Might have a great educational affect (and does not look too different from a filter or content warning).

> having the information is only one part of the solution, the issue is that we can't tell search engines that some part of the page is not to be indexed. I have not found a way yet to exclude replies/parent posts from search results without also making them completely unavailable to logged-out users.

Agreed that search indexing is all-or-nothing.  One approach is to mark the page for any thread with a non-searchable reply as "noindex"; if replies aren't consenting to being searchable, the original poster's preference shouldn't override that.

> Might we best let go of the idea that we present threads at all to unauthenticated users (which are in general a mix of _discoverable_ and _not discoverable_ posts), and simply present the one individual post for which the post URL refers, assuming that that one post is discoverable?
> 
> That way the search result would give the searcher exactly what they asked for, and if they wanted to see more context, they could log in.
> 
> The analogy for me is that of the embedded tweet - I see just the one (discoverable) tweet, not the entire thread. If I click on it and log in (or am already logged in), I see the whole thread.
> 
> I'd be OK with that. I realize its a "strong" UI choice rather than a minimal change from the current implementation. But imagine that it were behind a server feature flag, and admins had a conversation with their community like "We have the choice to present search engines and unauthenticated users with just those posts that their authors have elected to be discoverable, or we can present search engines and unauthenticated users with those posts in their thread context, which means that users who have opted out of discoverability will see their posts indexed because they engaged in a thread with a discoverable post." (I'm assuming the "enforcement" of discoverability is totally up to client implementations, which is itself weak soup, but I may be off base here).
> 
> This might strike an acceptable balance between discoverability and safety.

What you are describing is a recent change that makes Twitter a lot less useful and a lot more confusing to people who are not logged in. Furthermore, since Mastodon cannot ensure all replies federate everywhere and we are still lacking tools to alleviate that, a post's server remains the place where you are the most likely to have a complete view, and requiring you to register on every server would be very impractical.

> Furthermore, since Mastodon cannot ensure all replies federate everywhere and we are still lacking tools to alleviate that, a post's server remains the place where you are the most likely to have a complete view, and requiring you to register on every server would be very impractical.

Agreed.  By contrast, marking threads where the federated replies occur as "noindex" doesn't lead to these issues.  

Of course, badly-behaving search engines can still ignore noindex, so it's not an absolute protection, but the wording on the proposed privacy setting page highlighting that it doesn't _guarantee_ that posts are excluded covers this.

review_comments: Perhaps when using the `--only` CLI flag, we should automatically invoke both status indexes with the `statuses` option, otherwise it's inaccessible. But the CLI could be fixed/improved in a follow-up PR.
